title: Time Management Training and Student Stress

scenes.narration: Can a brief time management training help students feel less stressed and more in control of time during an ongoing semester? This study asked.
scenes.layout_description: Center a student between a tangled clock and a calmer planner, with orange arrows pointing toward calm.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn black ink student at a desk, one side showing a messy clock cloud, the other a neat calendar with yellow highlights, on cream background.

scenes.narration: The authors begin from a concern in prior research: university students often report stress, and time-related demands are described as a serious problem.
scenes.layout_description: Place a worried student under stacked papers and a large clock, with a small citation-style bubble labeled prior work.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal ink drawing of a student carrying books beneath an oversized clock and paper stack, orange stress lines, cream background.

scenes.narration: In the paper, time-related demands include high workload, time pressure, and the challenge of self-organized learning in higher education for many students.
scenes.layout_description: Show three simple icons in a row: workload, clock pressure, and a student planning alone.
scenes.visual_prompt: Three black ink vignette icons: tall book pile, alarm clock with orange ring, lone student with planner, yellow arrows linking them.

scenes.narration: The authors say research on time management training effectiveness is scarce, especially intervention studies with student samples and stress outcomes over time.
scenes.layout_description: Draw a mostly empty research shelf with one highlighted paper and a question mark.
scenes.visual_prompt: Ink line art of sparse bookshelf labeled with small paper shapes, one orange-highlighted study page, large question mark, cream background.

scenes.narration: Their research question was whether training could increase perceived control of time and reduce perceived stress, while perceived, self-reported demands stayed unchanged.
scenes.layout_description: Use a simple three-part balance: control rising, tension falling, demands level.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn scale-like diagram with upward arrow by clock, downward arrow by worried face, flat line by workload pile, orange accents.

scenes.narration: They used a non-equivalent dependent variable design: one trained group, two intended outcomes, and one control variable not expected to change after training.
scenes.layout_description: Show one group of students entering training, then splitting into three measured paths.
scenes.visual_prompt: Ink drawing of a small student group walking through an orange doorway labeled training, three arrows to simple icons: calm face, clock, workload.

scenes.narration: Forty-eight local undergraduate students began at a medium-sized German university, and 23 completed all questionnaires used in the main analyses reported here.
scenes.layout_description: Draw two student clusters, a larger starting group and a smaller completed group, connected by an arrow.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal line art of many simple student figures on the left, fewer on the right, orange arrow between, handwritten numbers above.

scenes.narration: Among the 23 completers, mean age was 23.30 years, SD=2.80, and about half of the participants were female, 52 %, in this sample.
scenes.layout_description: Place a small profile card beside a mixed group of students.
scenes.visual_prompt: Ink drawing of student silhouettes around a simple ID card with yellow highlights for age and percentage, cream background.

scenes.narration: Students attended a 4 h training in the middle of the semester, in groups of about ten, led by one experienced trainer.
scenes.layout_description: Show a trainer at a board with a small semicircle of students and a clock.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn classroom scene: one trainer pointing at a planner board, about ten simple student heads, small orange clock icon.

scenes.narration: Questionnaires were completed directly before training, 2 weeks after training, and 4 weeks after training, all within the same external context of the semester.
scenes.layout_description: Use a horizontal timeline with three clipboard points and one continuous semester bracket.
scenes.visual_prompt: Ink timeline across the slide with three clipboards, orange dots at before, 2 weeks, 4 weeks, yellow bracket underneath.

scenes.narration: The training focused on prioritizing, goal setting, strategy development, daily planning, and monitoring, drawing on the Häfner and Stock training approach described.
scenes.layout_description: Arrange five simple planning tools in a neat arc around a central student.
scenes.visual_prompt: Black ink student surrounded by checklist, target, steps, calendar, and tick marks; orange circles emphasize the five tools.

scenes.narration: First, students reflected on current academic and extracurricular activities, considered importance for study goals, and tried to define the most important ones.
scenes.layout_description: Show a student sorting task cards into a highlighted important pile.
scenes.visual_prompt: Ink drawing of hands moving small cards from a scattered table into an orange circled pile near a simple graduation-cap goal icon.

scenes.narration: Next, they defined concrete, challenging, proximal goals with deadlines, then developed steps, priorities, starting plans, and ways around possible obstacles toward goals.
scenes.layout_description: Draw a path from a starting dot to a target, with step stones and one obstacle.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn path with labeled step stones, target flag, small rock obstacle with an orange detour arrow, cream background.

scenes.narration: Later, daily planning asked what to do, when, where, and for how long; monitoring checked completed tasks and remaining work each day.
scenes.layout_description: Split the slide between a daily schedule and a checklist with some ticks.
scenes.visual_prompt: Ink line daily planner page on left and checklist on right, yellow tick marks, orange arrow from plan to checked tasks.

scenes.narration: Perceived stress was measured with the tension scale, covering mental fatigue, trouble relaxing, and nervousness; demands covered work amount and external duties.
scenes.layout_description: Show two labeled measuring cups: one for inner tension and one for demands outside the student.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal ink drawing of a student between two gauges: head with tired lines for tension, paper pile for demands, orange needle marks.

scenes.narration: Perceived control of time included feeling in control, estimating task time correctly, avoiding procrastination, and following one’s plans, as the paper describes.
scenes.layout_description: Place a student holding a clock and checklist, with procrastination shown as a crossed-out delay cloud.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn student calmly holding a clock and checklist; small snooze cloud crossed out in orange, yellow check marks.

scenes.narration: After training, reported use of time management strategies showed a nearly significant increase at 2 weeks and a significant increase at 4 weeks.
scenes.layout_description: Show a rising three-point line with the last point clearly highlighted.
scenes.visual_prompt: Ink chart with three dots rising slightly then more, second dot yellow, third dot orange, small planner icon beside line.

scenes.narration: At 2 weeks, the repeated-measurement MANOVA showed a significant overall time effect and significantly less stress measured by tension than before training.
scenes.layout_description: Draw a before-and-after tension meter, with the after needle lower.
scenes.visual_prompt: Two simple gauges labeled before and 2 weeks; before needle high, after needle lower, orange downward arrow, cream background.

scenes.narration: For perceived control of time at 2 weeks, the paper reports no significant increase, only a moderate tendency in the expected direction.
scenes.layout_description: Show a small upward arrow for control, drawn lightly rather than boldly.
scenes.visual_prompt: Ink drawing of a clock on a small platform rising slightly, pale yellow arrow upward, dotted orange outline indicating tentative change.

scenes.narration: At 4 weeks, the overall time effect was significant, and participants reported less tension and more perceived control of time than before training.
scenes.layout_description: Show two strong arrows: tension down and control up, both anchored at the 4-week point.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn 4-week marker with a worried-face meter dropping and a clock-control meter rising, orange arrows and yellow highlights.

scenes.narration: The control variable behaved as hypothesized: perceived, self-reported demands showed no significant changes at either 2 weeks or 4 weeks after training.
scenes.layout_description: Draw a flat line across three time points above an unchanged pile of work.
scenes.visual_prompt: Ink line graph with flat orange line over three dots, stable paper pile underneath, small clock icons for before, 2, and 4.

scenes.narration: Students with no or little prior time management experience seemed to profit more, especially for perceived stress, than students with moderate or some experience.
scenes.layout_description: Compare two simple student groups, with a larger improvement arrow for the no-or-little group.
scenes.visual_prompt: Two side-by-side groups of student icons; left group has bigger orange downward stress arrow, right group smaller yellow arrow.

scenes.narration: In the authors’ interpretation, prioritizing, goal setting, and strategy development might give students more orientation, which might reduce stress and foster control.
scenes.layout_description: Show a compass-like planner guiding a student through scattered tasks.
scenes.visual_prompt: Ink student following an orange compass arrow through loose task cards toward a target, with yellow path highlighting orientation.

scenes.narration: They also suggest daily planning might help initiate goal-oriented behaviour, while monitoring completed tasks might provide reinforcing information that might affect stress.
scenes.layout_description: Draw a plan page leading to completed check marks and a calmer face.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn calendar arrowing to checklist with tick marks, then to a calmer student face; orange and yellow highlights only.

scenes.narration: Because intended variables changed and demands did not, the authors argue the pattern supports training as the likely cause of changes reported.
scenes.layout_description: Place three evidence cards on a table, with two marked changed and one marked stable.
scenes.visual_prompt: Ink table with three cards: tension down, control up, demands flat; orange string connects cards back to a training icon.

scenes.narration: Still, they call the study preliminary: the sample was small, dropout was about half, and stronger designs with control groups are improvements.
scenes.layout_description: Show the findings under a magnifying glass beside a caution sign.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal line art of a small group of students viewed through magnifying glass, orange caution triangle, empty comparison group outline nearby.

scenes.narration: The takeaway is cautious: time management training might benefit undergraduate students’ well-being, but larger intervention studies are needed for more robust conclusions.
scenes.layout_description: End with a student walking from a planner toward a larger future research path.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn student holding planner, walking along orange path toward several blank study pages in the distance, yellow sunrise-like highlight on cream background.
